THOUGHT: This 44-year-old male with advanced, untreated HIV (CD4+ count 56/μL, high viral load >100,000 copies/mL) presents with subacute onset (1 week) of right leg weakness, unsteady gait, and falls — suggesting a focal or multifocal CNS process — superimposed on a 6-month progressive cognitive decline (disorientation, getting lost, apraxia-like difficulty with appliances), behavioral changes (paranoia, agitation, restlessness), and altered mental status (somnolence, confusion, disorientation to time/place). MRI shows disseminated, nonenhancing white matter lesions without mass effect — a key imaging clue. Nonenhancement argues against active toxoplasmosis (which typically enhances) and primary CNS lymphoma (which usually enhances and is often solitary or few in number). Cryptococcal antigen is negative, making cryptococcosis less likely (though early or IRIS-related cases can be antigen-negative). Toxoplasma IgG is positive, indicating prior exposure, but absence of enhancement makes reactivated toxo less likely. In the setting of profound immunosuppression, the combination of subcortical white matter disease, cognitive-behavioral decline, motor signs (hemiparesis), and lack of enhancement strongly points to HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder (HAND) — but HAND typically does not cause acute/subacute focal deficits like unilateral leg weakness or discrete white matter lesions on MRI. More acutely progressive white matter disease in advanced HIV raises concern for progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), caused by JC virus reactivation. PML classically presents with subacute focal neurological deficits (e.g., hemiparesis, ataxia, visual field cuts), cognitive/behavioral changes, and MRI showing asymmetric, nonenhancing, confluent white matter lesions — often involving subcortical U-fibers — without mass effect or edema. The disseminated, nonenhancing white matter lesions here are highly characteristic of PML. While PML is typically diagnosed via CSF JC virus PCR, the clinical-radiological correlation in this severely immunocompromised patient (CD4 < 100/μL) is highly specific. Other considerations — such as CNS lymphoma (usually enhances), CMV encephalitis (rare, often with ventriculitis), or HIV encephalitis (typically shows basal ganglia and deep gray matter involvement, not isolated white matter lesions) — are less consistent. The anemia, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia may reflect HIV-related bone marrow suppression or chronic inflammation but do not point to an alternative diagnosis. Thus, the most parsimonious and evidence-supported diagnosis is PML.

DIAGNOSIS: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy
